standard.title: Investigate needs and processes
standard.description: Investigate needs or opportunities for designing, and the materials, components, tools, equipment and processes needed to create designed solutions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore needs or opportunities for designing, and test materials, components, tools, equipment and processes to make designed solutions (AC9TDE4P01). They have explored and tested. They have not yet investigated systematically — the shift is from exploring/testing to purposeful investigation with a view to making design decisions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate needs or opportunities for designing and determine the materials, components, tools, equipment and processes required — including sustainability considerations and comparative evaluation of options.

nodes.label: Investigating a need or opportunity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate a need or opportunity for designing by gathering information from multiple sources and identifying what a solution must achieve
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a need or opportunity and investigate it using at least two sources (e.g. surveying users, examining existing solutions, researching online) — summarising what a solution must achieve
nodes.typical_width: Survey users in a school or community context to identify a need; investigate existing solutions from around the world to assess suitability; identify the key requirements a designed solution must meet — including functional, social and sustainability requirements
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' traditional fibre sources as potential commercial solutions for biodegradable string or rope — researching the materials, systems, components and processes needed to develop them commercially
Investigate small-space gardening solutions from different countries and judge their suitability for the local environment — explaining what factors determine suitability

Survey school community members about a specific need (e.g. more shade, a security system for the community garden, a community meal) — documenting needs and constraints that a designed solution must address

response_modes.reason: Students often investigate a single, self-identified need without testing it against actual users. Multiple investigation contexts — each with different stakeholders and information sources — build the habit of grounding needs in evidence rather than assumption.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations fibre/commercial viability direction is rich — it requires students to investigate across material science, sustainability, and commercial viability simultaneously, and situates investigation in a real economic opportunity with social dimensions.
success_criteria: Identifies a need or opportunity with evidence from at least two sources
States what a solution must achieve — not just what is wrong
nodes.hinge_reason: Thin investigation in N1 cascades into every downstream phase — design ideas (P02), material selection (N2, P03), and evaluation criteria (P04) all depend on having accurately characterised what the solution must achieve. An underspecified need produces solutions that solve the wrong problem.

nodes.label: Determining required materials, components and processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can determine what materials, components, tools, equipment and processes are needed to create a designed solution — and compare options
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two options for a key material or component and explain which is more appropriate for the design intention, considering at least one sustainability factor
nodes.typical_width: Test or research materials, components, tools and equipment to determine which are appropriate for the design; compare options on multiple criteria including function, cost, availability, safety and environmental impact; explain how minimising material use and managing waste affects production decisions
wider: Investigate how to minimise material use and manage waste by comparing the environmental and social impacts of alternative approaches — e.g. repurposing an old item of clothing to create a carry bag versus buying a new one
Deconstruct a product (e.g. a robotic weeder, a vacuum cleaner) to identify its components and explain the function of each — connecting component design to the product's overall purpose
Investigate complementary parts of a working system by identifying how each component's function depends on the others — explaining why changing one component would affect the whole system

response_modes.reason: Students typically select materials based on familiarity rather than systematic comparison. The reasoning scaffold — identify options → compare on criteria → justify selection — makes material selection a design decision rather than a default choice.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two options for a material or component
Compares options using at least one criterion and justifies the selection
